title: The Night Journey to Kundina
story:
Rukmini, the princess of Kundina, had sent a brahmana — a priest, trusted and learned — across the country to beg Krishna to come for her before her family could marry her to Shishupala, the king of Cedi. The road from Dwaraka to Kundina usually took days. Krishna crossed it in a single night.

He heard the brahmana out, and he did not hide what the message had done to him. "I too," he said, "cannot sleep at night for her sake." And he said plainly what he meant to do: he would bring her back, and in the doing of it he would crush the wicked kings who stood in his way. There was no council called, no army mustered. The chariot was made ready; the four horses — Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa, and Balahaka — were yoked; and Daruka, his charioteer, took the reins. Krishna seated the brahmana beside him, and they went out through the gates of Dwaraka while the city slept.

Through the dark they flew, over river and plain, with the princess's words still hanging in the air between them. By the time the sun rose, Krishna was within the borders of Vidarbha — and no one in Kundina knew he had come.

In Kundina no one had slept either, but for a different reason. The city was being made ready for a wedding. Bhishmaka, the king, led by love for his son Rukmi, had ordered the streets swept and sprinkled and the crossings cleaned; garlands, perfumes, and bright garments appeared on every side. He worshipped the ancestors, the gods, and the priests according to the rites. The bride was bathed and adorned with the ceremonies of good fortune, and the foremost brahmanas chanted over her for her protection the ancient hymns of the Sama, the Rig, and the Yajur. Gifts of gold and silver cloth and sesame mixed with jaggery were given out, and the whole city put on its finest face for the day to come.

The guests who arrived showed what the day was for. Damaghosha, the king of Cedi, came for his son Shishupala with herds of great elephants and chariots hung with gold, and Bhishmaka, the lord of Vidarbha, went out to receive him with honor. With him came Shalva, and Jarasandha of Magadha, and Dantavakra, and Viduratha — kings who hated Krishna and his elder brother Balarama, and who were determined to give the bride to the prince of Cedi. "If Krishna comes," they resolved among themselves, "we will fight him, and we will fight him together."

Word of that muster traveled the roads, and it reached Balarama. Flooded with love for his brother, he gathered a great force and set out after him — so that the man who had ridden ahead with a single chariot now had an army on the road behind him.

And all the while, in the inner apartments of Kundina, the bride-to-be was counting the hours toward a wedding she had never wanted — hoping, with everything in her, that the man she had sent for would come in time.
reflection: The line that stays with the reader is Krishna's admission that he, too, could not sleep for her. The great dash to Kundina is easy to read as rescue or romance; the source quietly makes it mutual, and lets the two longings answer each other across the country.
next_story_tease: In Kundina the bride-to-be had heard that Krishna had come — but the wedding was still a night away, and she had not yet seen him.
hero_scene: Krishna's chariot flying across moonlit plains at full gallop, Daruka driving, the brahmana holding on beside him, the four horses — Shaibya, Sugriva, Meghapushpa, and Balahaka — stretched to their limit through the night.
visual_elements: Krishna's chariot racing through the night
the four horses at full gallop
the wedding preparations of Kundina in the distance
a mood of urgent love and resolve
